items.title: Alberta bill poses potential risk to TC Energy growth plans, CIBC analysts say
items.description: Analysts at CIBC Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.’s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.

items._ogDesc: Analysts at CIBC Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.’s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.
items.body:
CALGARY — Analysts at CIBC Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.’s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.

The bill, if passed, would enable the provincial government to set up Crown entities to plan or build new natural gas pipelines to meet booming demand from data centres, the oilsands and other industries.

The Alberta government says such a move would be a last resort if the private sector can’t meet the pipeline capacity needs, and has raised concerns about the adequacy of TC’s expansion plans.

  • Latest updates on company news here

CIBC analysts Robert Catellier and Rogan Anantharajah say in a report that provincial involvement could complicate the timing and economics of future expansions on the NGTL system.

They note that NGTL, which spans much of Alberta and connects into neighbouring provinces, is federally regulated, raising questions over how far Alberta’s powers would extend.

Last week, TC Energy announced plans to expand NGTL, including with a new 370-kilometre pipeline connecting gas to the oilsands region, and additional loops and compressor units.

TC also said it plans to launch 1.3 billion cubic feet per day in new service offerings as early as January, for delivery between 2030 and 2032.

“Ultimately, we view (the legislation) as creating potential risks to securing growth rather than undermining the entire NGTL business. While the situation warrants monitoring, we believe the risk remains largely confined to headlines at this stage,” the CIBC analysts said.

TC has spent $15 billion in the last decade on expansion projects on NGTL.

In a letter to Premier Danielle Smith obtained by The Canadian Press, TC chief executive François Poirier warned against legislation that would undermine the integrated infrastructure that TC and fellow energy shipper and distributor ATCO Ltd. operate.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

“Legislation that proposes overriding integration would create significant market instability. The uncertainty created by the government’s proposed measures would mean companies and customers cannot make long-term capital and contracting decisions with confidence,” Poirier wrote.

“We struggle to see how we can progress the new capacity offering of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet per day announced on Nov. 16, 2026, if legislation overrides the integrated NGTL-ATCO system. The proposed capacity offering that has been announced is premised on integration remaining intact.”

A spokesperson for Atco said its power and pipeline unit, Canadian Utilities, is reviewing the legislation.

“The integrated system was intended to maximize the use of existing infrastructure, support efficient investment, and provide reliable service for customers across the province. Canadian Utilities remains ready to invest in the infrastructure needed to meet customer demand and support Alberta’s continued growth,” the statement said.

“We will review the legislation through the lens of how it supports these outcomes for our customers. Throughout that process, our focus will remain on delivering safe, reliable, and affordable energy service for Albertans.”

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon is pushing back against criticism of new land seizure powers proposed for a high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.
items.body:
Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon is pushing back against criticism of new land seizure powers proposed for a high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.

MacKinnon says the enhanced expropriation abilities detailed in draft legislation would allow Ottawa to fast-track steps that could otherwise become bogged down for years and insists that “there is no removal of due process.”

The comments comes after the federal government included in a 519-page procedural motion on Friday measures that would expand its power to lock down property rights along the corridor, such as barring sale or work on a given lot for years.

The move builds on a law passed in June that enabled the government to expropriate land without public hearings, among other reforms.

Ontario Conservative MP Michael Barrett says the latest changes would replace the existing Expropriation Act with a separate regime for high-speed rail, compounding concerns about cost and disruption to rural communities in eastern Ontario and Quebec.

The high-speed rail project would see trains running between the two provincial capitals at 300 kilometres per hour at a projected cost of between $60 billion and $90 billion, with work set to start on the Montreal-Ottawa leg by 2030.

items.title: Macklem admits Bank of Canada offered mixed messaging on core inflation in past
items.description: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem waits to appear at the finance committee in Ottawa, Monday, May 4, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.

The federal government and the Bank of Canada renewed the central bank’s five-year mandate earlier this month and maintained the target for two per cent annual inflation, as measured by Statistics Canada’s consumer price index, or CPI.

The central bank maintains a one-to-three per cent band around that target, which offers some wiggle room to execute monetary policy.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem spoke to a business crowd in Toronto on Tuesday where he hailed the two per cent target as a “clear and well-understood objective” since it was implemented in 1995.

Anchoring its policy rate decisions on that inflation target helped the Bank of Canada tame the post-COVID surge in inflation, Macklem argued in prepared remarks. But he acknowledged that Canadians didn’t respond well to inflation and the rate hikes it necessitated.

“For many Canadians, it was their first experience with high inflation. And they didn’t like it. As we reviewed our framework, we held consultations across the country to hear from Canadians. We heard a lot of anger,” Macklem said.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The head of the Bank of Canada acknowledged in his speech that the central bank could have done a better job in the post-pandemic period, which saw inflation pressures compound after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Monetary policymakers were “too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy,” Macklem said.

He also acknowledged that the Bank of Canada has, at times, put focus on different measures of core inflation to track underlying price trends.

The Bank of Canada previously downplayed its preferred measures of core inflation, CPI-trim and CPI-median, as it tried to gauge how supply shocks were affecting the economy.

“We wanted to be transparent about where we saw inflation pressures and where we did not. But we weren’t as clear as we hoped,” Macklem said.

“Canadians found it confusing when we discussed measures that strip out volatile prices such as food and gasoline. After all, these are important parts of the family budget. And financial market participants sometimes felt that we were moving the inflation goalposts.”

Excluding the right measures can help give the Bank of Canada a clearer picture of inflation trends and cut through temporary forces pushing prices higher, Macklem said.

Now, the Bank of Canada will put its focus back on an old measure called CPIX, which excludes eight fixed sets of items from the inflation calculation to provide a consistent benchmark of how prices are evolving.

The Bank of Canada used CPIX to guide monetary policy decisions from 2001 to 2016. Some of the items excluded from CPIX are gasoline, mortgage interest costs and fruits and vegetables.

The central bank will retain what’s called CPI-trim as its other core measure, which strips out the items seeing the most extreme price changes in each month.

Macklem explained that, while the Bank of Canada’s updated core metrics can help monetary policymakers see where prices are headed, keeping overall inflation at two per cent remains the central bank’s north star.

“Total CPI inflation is our target, and it will be front and centre in all our communications. Various indicators help us understand where inflation is headed and the risks around that forecast. But they are inputs to our analysis, not targets,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

items.title: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after historic outage, internal memos show: Reuters exclusive
items.description: Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A computer screen shows the Microsoft support page in London, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Kirsty Wigglesworth</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters.
items.body:
Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters.

The Nov. 12-13 outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms and disrupted airline communications, fuelling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.

Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption.

The Code Red signified the most severe and urgent alert to address weaknesses in Microsoft’s engineering and operational practices after the outage disrupted Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 products.

It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday.

Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

‘Fog of war’

Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company’s workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded.

Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

“Our work doesn’t end when service is restored. Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority,” a company spokesperson told Reuters when contacted about the memos.

Recovery target

As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms.

Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly.

Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews.

The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions.

Slow patch developments

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur.

In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said “urgent patches to our M365 Core services” took too long to deploy worldwide.

“In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” he wrote.

Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; editing by Arpan Varghese and Anil D’Silva

items.description: Best Buy raised its annual comparable sales growth target, betting on robust demand during the holiday season as customers spend on AI-driven gadgets.

items._ogDesc: Best Buy raised its annual comparable sales growth target, betting on robust demand during the holiday season as customers spend on AI-driven gadgets.
items.body:
Best Buy raised its annual comparable sales growth target on Tuesday, betting on robust demand during the holiday shopping season as customers spend on new AI-enabled phones and TVs as well as wearable technology such as smart glasses.

“We’re seeing the emerging categories bucket ... health rings, AI glasses, and trading cards and collectibles are driving about a full point of comp (comparable sales growth) for us,” CEO Jason Bonfig told Reuters.

Affluent consumers have been splurging on pricier nice-to-have products across categories from dual-screen phones to Coach handbags, as they lock in gains from stock market portfolios and investments in assets such as real estate.

  • Latest updates on company news here

In contrast, lower- and middle-income consumers have sharply pulled back spending, with inflation and high gas prices crimping budgets, exacerbating a K-shaped effect among US consumers this year.

Consumers have also been upgrading their phones, laptops and other gadgets for AI-enabled options, often at higher price points, driving an upgrade cycle for the electronics retailer.

Best Buy said it saw “significant strength” in its business above the US$1,500 price point in the three months through October, when total comparable sales jumped 6.1 per cent and handily beat estimates of 2.3 per cent growth.

The company was working within its supply chain to dull the hit from higher fuel costs, said Bonfig, who took over as CEO earlier this month.

Retailers across the board have warned of higher freight costs this year as the U.S. war on Iran drags up oil prices.

Best Buy now expects annual comparable sales to rise between 3.4 and four per cent, compared with its earlier target of 1.9 to three per cent growth. Its stock rose about two per cent in morning trading.

Comparable sales growth driven by computing and phones is a positive sign for electronics at Walmart, Target and Costco heading into the holiday shopping season, said Stifel analyst Michael Montani.

Higher memory chip costs have driven up product prices, but computing demand remained resilient, Best Buy executives said on a post-earnings call.

Trade-ins on older products, credit card financing options and some promotions were levers Best Buy was pulling to support sales in the category, executives added.

Best Buy’s total revenue rose 5.8 per cent to US$10.24 billion in the third quarter, beating estimates of US$9.90 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

As customers prepared for the launch of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” the much-awaited installment in Take-Two Interactive’s flagship franchise, Best Buy saw growth in gaming hardware and accessories in the third quarter, Bonfig said.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings per share target to between US$6.90 and US$7.05, after quarterly adjusted earnings of US$1.62 per share topped estimates.

items.title: Nvidia, Anthropic and other AI stocks get back to tumbling and drag the U.S. market lower
items.description: Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are leading the U.S. market lower once again, even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Aug. 10, 2022. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, file)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are leading the U.S. market lower once again, even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are leading the U.S. market lower once again on Tuesday. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising, along with confidence among Americans in the economy.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent after dropping as much as 1.4 per cent earlier, and it’s heading toward its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks led the way lower in a turnaround from Monday’s surge and dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.3 per cent, as of 10:05 a.m. Eastern time.

But the majority of U.S. stocks were nevertheless rising, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 271 points, or 0.5 per cent.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

It’s the latest swing for a market that has been mostly sinking since setting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ 401(k) accounts because AI stocks have grown so big that they’ve become Wall Street’s most influential sector.

While the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang does bring back a charismatic leader who championed and helped build the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it.

At the same time, high interest rates in the bond market caused in part by the war with Iran are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres.

To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour.

For now, at least, the momentum is back downward.

Nvidia fell 6.6 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts.

CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, sank 9 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, fell 4.6 per cent.

And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, tumbled 7.4 per cent to drop below US$83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as US$115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Such drops were powerful enough to offset gains for the slight majority of stocks on Wall Street. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected.

Companies in industries across the economy also continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. That helped the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 to rise.

Dollar Tree climbed 11.3 per cent after reporting better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than a year earlier, and more of them came than last year.

Kohl’s rallied 13 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected.

The retailers are among the latest companies to join the long list of big U.S. companies delivering bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet.

Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated.

  • Latest updates on investing here

In the bond market, Treasury yields slipped as investors moved into investments seen as safer bets. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.91 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday.

That was despite a rise in oil prices, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.8 per cent to US$88.26. It’s been yo-yoing between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

items.title: James Moore: Some urgent questions for Mark Carney before a tariff deal with the U.S.
items.description: Former senior cabinet minister James Moore challenges the federal government's trade strategy, pressing Prime Minister Mark Carney to answer critical questions before locking Canada into a permanent tariff agreement with the Trump administration.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump and Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney speak at the G7 working luncheon, during the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Christopher Katsarov]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Former senior cabinet minister James Moore challenges the federal government's trade strategy, pressing Prime Minister Mark Carney to answer critical questions before locking Canada into a permanent tariff agreement with the Trump administration.
items.body:
James Moore is a former federal cabinet minister under prime minister Stephen Harper and is a contributing columnist for CTVNews.ca.

Negotiating a trade deal with the U.S. has always been a high-stakes chess match.

I don’t envy the task resting on the shoulders of Prime Minister Mark Carney and his core team, including Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Ambassador Mark Wiseman, Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, and Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia.

In Canada’s history, there have been few issues where economics, national pride, sovereignty, pragmatism, security and law are in such violent conflict that landing an ideal outcome is effectively impossible; but finding a credible pathway is fraught with endless complications and consequences that it can break one’s mind.

But here we are. And our chosen decision makers have to lead and make the tough calls in strategizing Canada’s path forward in the remaining two years of the tariff-loving Trump administration that is growing more erratic and unhinged by the day on nearly every front.

Meanwhile Canada’s economy and key sectors struggle with Section 232 tariffs on autos, aluminum, steel and lumber and Section 338 tariffs on other sectors, and Canada United States Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) re-negotiations on the horizon all triggering uncertainty about jobs and investment decisions and a time when we can afford it least.

There is growing chatter of a coming announcement of some form of a new “trade/tariff deal” with the Trump administration, and I am filled with questions.

What is the actual tariff rate, sector by sector, and how does it compare with what Canada faced before 2025? Will you publish the full text before Canada is bound by it? Have affected industries been consulted so they can assess what new rates would mean and whether they will cause comfort and stability for their business decisions in the coming year? Will Parliament have a chance to vote on this?

About 90% of U.S. imports from Canada have stayed tariff-free, largely thanks to CUSMA. Does this deal put that at risk by validating tariffs onto goods that were exempt? Are we sure they consented-to tariffs would be circumscribed and not expanded by definitional interpretation later?

After years of saying tariffs between allies are unacceptable, why is accepting a new permanent minimum tariff now a “win”?

Name one thing the United States is giving up in this deal that it can’t take back tomorrow if Donald Trump has a tantrum and wants to?

The trust gap

Trump has broken deals before, including his own CUSMA. What in this agreement stops a new tariff threat next week or month, or anytime between now and the end of his term? Why should we believe him if he says he won’t? Why do you believe him? Is there a snapback, a dispute mechanism, anything enforceable to point to?

When forest fire smoke next summer agitates him, or if he grows tired of Canada for any reason at all, or if Peter Navarro or Stephen Miller convince him with lies that Canada has been treating America unfairly and needs to be hit with a new tariff, why should we think he won’t do so?

America has just elected a new Congress led by members of both the House of Representatives and the Senate who campaigned against Trump’s tariffs. Why wouldn’t Canada wait for the new Congress to be sworn into office before making any deal with a White House whose trade and tariff policy was so firmly rebuked by American voters?

Opposition to tariffs on Canada is a more popular political stance than almost any other contemporary policy question being debated. Tariffs are massively unpopular in the Republican Party, the Democratic Party, with independent voters, with farmers, with the business community – momentum is clearly on the side of Canada and against the side of Trump’s failed tariff policies. Why would we accept Trump’s tariffs now?

Congressional leverage

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become Speaker in January, celebrated the House vote in February to “detonate the Trump tariffs on Canada,” and since the midterms has put restoring Congress’s authority over tariffs on his 100-day agenda.

Why would we slow momentum towards this pro-trade and anti-tariff agenda? Should he go tools-down now if we are going to accept a minimum tariff threshold for certain Canadian exports to the United States? Why should they fight?

It is said that Democrats lack a veto-proof majority, so Trump could veto any repeal effort. Yes, but a Congress that can pass a repeal with bipartisan votes changes the leverage at the table and will have the long-term benefit of stigmatizing this terrible Trump tariff policy for the coming primaries in both the Republican and Democratic Parties, and could drive bipartisan momentum toward long-term trade and tariff reconciliation between Canada and the United States.

So let it happen. Unleash the debate and have confidence that the massive weight of economics and public opinion opposition to tariffs will win the day. Why sign before we have seen it play out?

  • More opinions and expert analyses

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming chair of the Senate Finance Committee, has signaled the Canadian tariffs will be an early target when he takes the gavel. Should he now not do that, given we are accepting the premise that some Trump tariffs are okay?

In August you said America’s signature is written “in pencil.” Canadians agreed and believed you. Why should we believe that Donald Trump’s signature is now written in ink?

None of these questions is meant to diminish how hard this file is, or the effort of Prime Minister Carney, Minister LeBlanc, Ambassador Wiseman, Janice Charette, Michael Sabia and their team, who have carried an impossible burden with skill and patriotism.

But a deal that writes tariffs into the relationship between two of the closest allies in the world is a decision that will outlast this administration, and Canadians deserve to have these questions answered before it is signed, not after.

If the answers are good, the prime minister should have no trouble giving them; if they are not, the best deal may be the one we wait for.

items.description: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.content: <p>Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638367747040950607.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.body:
The Canadian mortgage market is not short of challenges in 2026, but for Calgary-based broker Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group (pictured top), difficulty and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.

Singh describes a Canadian mortgage market shaped by affordability pressures, bond market volatility, and a record renewal wave, with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) projecting 1.15 million mortgage renewals in 2026, the largest concentration in recent history.

"I would describe 2026 as a year of adjustment and opportunity," Singh told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Compared to last year, I've noticed clients becoming much more strategic about their mortgage decisions, whether that's purchasing, refinancing or renewing."

Navigating a shifting lending landscape

Tightening lender guidelines and heightened scrutiny around income verification and debt servicing have defined the operational challenge of 2026 for Singh.

"With bond market volatility, changing lender guidelines and increased scrutiny around income and debt servicing, mortgage brokers need to be more knowledgeable and adaptable than ever," he said.

"I've always believed our greatest value comes from understanding the client's complete financial picture and having the experience and relationships to find solutions when traditional lending doesn't quite fit."

His assessment aligns with CMP's latest market analysis of the risks facing Canadian mortgage brokers.

Lindsay Zwart, Equifax Canada's director of solutions for mortgage and housing, reinforced the point at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

"Risking a borrower in 2026 does not look the same as risking a borrower in 2016, in 2019, and in 2020," Zwart told delegates.

"As a broker, your two most valuable currencies are your time and your reputation in the industry with your lenders."

Mortgage Professionals Canada's 2026 consumer survey, cited in CMP's 2026 Brokers on Lenders special report, puts broker market share at 38% in 2025, a six-percentage-point annual gain and the highest level on record.

Looking ahead to 2027

Singh expects confidence to build gradually rather than through dramatic rate reductions.

"I'm cautiously optimistic about 2027," he said.

"I believe we'll see opportunities as economic conditions evolve, buyers regain confidence and homeowners continue reviewing their mortgage options. I don't necessarily anticipate dramatic interest rate reductions, but I do expect clients to become increasingly comfortable making financial decisions rather than waiting indefinitely for the perfect market."

CMP's annual ranking of Canada's 75 best mortgage brokers — professionals who collectively moved more than $10 billion — illustrates the relational model Singh champions.

"Whether it's reaching out six to nine months before renewal, conducting annual mortgage reviews or simply checking in, I believe the brokers who invest in relationships, education and proactive mortgage management will be the ones who really thrive in 2027."

The motivation goes deeper than deal volume.

"At the end of the day, we're not just arranging mortgages; we're helping people build wealth, achieve homeownership and make better financial decisions for their families. That's what keeps me passionate about this business," Singh said.

items.title: Ontario mortgage arrears near crisis peak as rates take toll
items.description: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.content: <p>A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639311370259041851.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.body:
Canadian consumers are expected to "bend, but not break" – but nowhere is that strain more visible than in Ontario, where mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic norms.

A November report by TD Economics economist Maria Solovieva, CFA, finds the province's arrears rate hit 0.34% in August, approaching the 0.43% peak of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) from a pre-pandemic baseline of just 0.12%.

While national real consumer spending grew at a nearly 3% pace through the first half of 2026, Solovieva cautions that "solid spending growth masks pockets of financial strain, particularly in Ontario."

Consumer insolvency rates, though still below GFC-era highs, have trended upward since the rate-hiking cycle began in 2022, and the most recent reading "suggests a renewed upward pressure, warranting close monitoring," the report states.

TransUnion's financial stress indicator, also tracked by the Bank of Canada, reached a new high of 2.23% in Q2 2026, roughly 25 basis points above its pre-pandemic average. 

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

What rising arrears mean for brokers and their clients

Ontario's vulnerability traces to the pandemic housing boom. As CMP's analysis of Ontario and BC delinquency trends confirmed, buyers near the 2021–22 price peak carry larger balances and thinner equity, while BC 's rate of increase has started to slow.

The TD Economics report notes that "even at today's elevated rate, roughly one in 300 Ontario mortgages is in arrears," and that "the greatest vulnerability likely lies among those who purchased near the 2021–22 housing market peak, when prices were highest and equity cushions may be thinnest."

Leah Zlatkin, licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in May that the data demands vigilance: "Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," Zlatkin said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Statistics Canada data cited in the TD Economics report show more than 35% of households in Oshawa, Windsor, and Hamilton, Ontario are struggling to meet their financial needs – the highest rates among Canada's largest cities – with all three cities reporting unemployment above the national average.

Labour market is the bigger swing factor

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points in October, with another increase expected in January 2027.

Variable-rate mortgages account for a historically high 35% of outstanding mortgages in Canada.

The report estimates roughly $115 in additional annual mortgage servicing costs relative to earlier forecasts; in Ontario, the figure rises to approximately $140 annually – on top of a servicing burden already around $2,250 above the national average.

Those increases are "unlikely to be the straw that breaks the camel's back, but they represent another expense for households whose budgets are already stretched by higher inflation," Solovieva writes.

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told CMP earlier this year that a dramatic escalation remained unlikely: "I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it's going to be a slow grind," he said.

"It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales. At the end of the day, the banks and lenders out there are in business to help homeowners out and lend them money, not to foreclose on homes."

TD Economics forecasts Ontario's arrears to plateau near mid-2027, declining in the second half of the year as employment conditions improve.

The principal risk is clear: "if weak hiring gives way to widespread job losses, pushing the unemployment rate higher, mortgage arrears could rise further and remain elevated for longer."

For now, the report's conclusion stands – "households in Ontario and across Canada are expected to bend, but not break."

items.title: MCAN Financial puts its support behind brokers at the CMAs
items.description: Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards
items.content: <p>Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639217273141247328.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards
items.body:
MCAN Financial Group is backing the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) as sponsor for one of its most important honours, the MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, with the 20th edition of the ceremony set to take place on Wednesday (November 25) at Rebel Toronto.

The awards are an important opportunity to celebrate the people behind an industry that’s as essential as ever to helping Canadians achieve their homebuying dreams, according to MCAN’s director of corporate brand and marketing Kim Mercer.

“MCAN is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards because at its core this industry is about people,” she told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The CMAs give us a chance to set competition aside and celebrate what we’re all working toward: helping Canadians make it home.”

With mortgage professionals set to congregate in Toronto from across the whole country for the star-studded ceremony, Mercer said the evening was also about connection.

“It’s an opportunity to recognize the brokers, teams and partners who show up for their clients and communities every day, and the people and partnerships that keep our industry moving forward,” she said.

“It’s also a fun night to reconnect with colleagues, celebrate success, and cheer on the award nominees.”

Mercer said the MCAN team is especially excited about the nomination of Cam Dellipizzi, one of 10 shortlisted for Lender BDM of the Year (Prime).

The value of relationships

The case for celebrating excellence comes back to relationships, Mercer said, at a time when the connection between brokers and lenders has arguably never been more important.

“This is a relationship-driven business, and excellence often comes down to how many people show up for their clients and partners, especially when the market is complex,” she said.

The event takes place at a significant moment for the mortgage and housing markets, with affordability challenges and rising interest rates continuing to present hurdles for Canadian homebuyers and owners.

That’s part of the reason mortgage professionals are such a valuable component of the housing sector, Mercer suggested. “After a year of uncertainty, it’s important to celebrate what makes this industry such a powerful part of Canadians’ homeownership journeys: the people,” she said.

“Recognizing great work gives us a chance to celebrate the people raising the bar and reminds all of us what great service and partnership can look like.”

MCAN’s 2026 and 2027 focuses

With 2027 just around the corner, the industry is reflecting on the year that’s been and looking ahead to what’s in store for the coming 12 months.

Mercer paid tribute to the brokers working with MCAN to help Canadians navigate the current market, and highlighted opportunities in store next year. “We’re incredibly grateful for the support of our broker partners and the trust they place in us to deliver for their clients,” she said.

“This year challenged all of us to be more flexible and thoughtful about how we help Canadians navigate homeownership. For MCAN, that means continuing to listen and invest in our people, products, technology and experience, making it easier for brokers to find responsible solutions for real-life client needs.”

On the product side, Mercer said MCAN had worked to keep its mortgage solutions in step with what’s most important to brokers in a constantly evolving market. “A big focus for us has been making sure our mortgage solutions keep pace with what brokers are actually seeing across Canada,” she said.

And the lender has also invested in how brokers work with it. “We’ve continued investing in the overall partner experience through our regional teams, technology, clearer pricing and programs like SCORE and ICON that create value beyond the transaction,” she said.

Meanwhile, the company has kept its partner events going in 2026, with Summits and Connects continuing in Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Spain. Next year’s destination is Porto. “Great partnerships should deliver great business and a little fun along the way,” Mercer said.

As the industry prepares to celebrate its top performers at the CMAs – and toast the importance of strong connections and partnerships – Mercer said the human side of the business remains paramount.

“One thing that continues to stand out to us is that every mortgage file represents a person, a family and a story,” she said. “We believe the good stuff happens when brokers and lenders understand that full picture and work together to find a responsible path forward. That’s the kind of partnership we want to keep building in 2027.”

items.title: Finmo's Sidekick: the AI assistant that knows your deals
items.description: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.content: <p>Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_639307939243156766.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.body:
Most brokers have tried AI tools to draft emails and answer quick questions. What they haven't had is an AI assistant that knows their deals and can work on them.

Lendesk built Sidekick to close that gap. Sidekick launched in open beta at Finmo Momentum 2026 on November 24 and it's a new AI assistant inside Finmo, Lendesk's mortgage origination platform. It runs in a chat panel next to the broker's deals, where it reads the application and documents, makes updates on request, and looks up lender rates and guidelines. The broker never has to leave the deal.

“We wanted to give brokers a tool that actually works the deal, instead of just surfacing information about it. Sidekick knows the deal, knows the lenders, and takes on the admin, so brokers can spend more time with clients,” said Carter Zimmerman, president of Lendesk.

From single tasks to the whole deal

Each of Finmo's earlier AI tools did one job. In 2024, Finmo added AI deal create, which builds a new application from an email chain, call transcript or notes, and AI fill from document, which pulls property details from an MLS listing into the deal. This year Finmo added AI down payment verification and income verification, which cut hours of document review down to minutes.

Sidekick works differently. It doesn't run one fixed process. It can help with any task a broker does in Finmo: building and editing deals, managing documents, running down payment and income verification, calculating GDS/TDS, and researching lenders.

“Our first AI tools each solved one problem well. Sidekick ties them together,” Zimmerman said. “For the first time, a broker can ask for help the way they’d ask a colleague and get it across the whole deal.”

Ask Sidekick to organize and review a deal’s documents, and it renames files consistently, moves them into the right document conditions, and adds any missing conditions. It then runs down payment and income verification.

Ask Sidekick which rental income approach works best for a conventional deal, and it compares lenders’ add-back and offset policies using Lender Spotlight. It estimates the impact on GDS/TDS and compares available rates and requirements, helping identify the best fit and the lowest-rate option that meets the lender’s stated qualifying limits.

“Sidekick takes what you thought was a B deal and turns it into an A deal,” said Joe Tomkins, Director of User Development & Enablement at Lendesk.

Placing the deal

Sidekick connects to Lender Spotlight, so it can match a deal against lender policies and pull current rates. The "Place this deal" flow works the deal the way an experienced broker would. It grades the deal, screens lenders on their guidelines, and compares rates. Then it gives one recommendation, with a short list of alternatives.

“Finding the right lender for a deal takes experience, plus a lot of checking rates and guidelines across dozens of lenders,” Zimmerman said. “Sidekick handles the checking in one request, so brokers get to the right shortlist faster.”

The broker makes the call

By default, Sidekick asks before it changes anything. Each update, whether it's an edit to the application or a credit pull, shows up as an approval card with the exact change. Nothing is saved until the broker approves it. Read-only tasks, like reviewing the deal or running GDS/TDS numbers, happen right away.

Sidekick also works within the broker's own permissions, so it can only see and do what that broker already can in Finmo — and brokers can delete their chat history at any time.

“In mortgages, trust isn't optional,” Zimmerman said. “That's why Sidekick shows every change before it's made. The broker is always in control.”

Sidekick is available now in open beta, free while the beta runs. Brokers already on Finmo can ask their team admin to turn it on through Finmo support. Brokers new to Finmo can sign up and request access when they join.

items.title: New natural gas legislation could allow Alberta to appoint provincial authority
items.description: New legislation tabled in the legislature Monday allows Alberta to appoint a Crown entity that could participate in natural gas transmission.
items._ogDesc: New legislation tabled in the legislature Monday allows Alberta to appoint a Crown entity that could participate in natural gas transmission.
items.body:
New legislation tabled in the legislature Monday allows Alberta to appoint a Crown entity that could participate in natural gas transmission.

The province says the current natural gas transmission system (NGTL), owned by TC Energy, is fully subscribed until 2029 and there is uncertainty around its capacity beyond 2030.

“Under these conditions, gas sellers can’t sell, gas buyers can’t buy,” said Energy Minister Brian Jean at a press conference. “Our current transmission infrastructure has failed to keep pace with Alberta’s growth and our ambitions.”

Jean went on to say the Natural Gas Infrastructure Act will give the province the tools to plan, encourage competition and support the development of natural gas infrastructure to best serve Albertans.

While the province is looking to get its natural gas out to the marketplace, the minister said he wants to guarantee Albertans the first chance to reap the benefits.

“We want to make sure Albertans who are facing a lot of bills right now, that natural gas, which is the backbone to our energy and our jobs and just about everything else, is affordable,” said Jean. “As we move forward, we’ll see whether or not industry replies to the needs.”

He added that a Crown entity would only participate as a last resort.

“Alberta’s gas collection and transmission systems, the current NGTL system, was originally built by the government,” said Jean. “With this legislation, we are putting the framework in place to support responsible growth and make the most of our province’s extraordinary potential.”

The act also allows the province to designate critical natural gas infrastructure systems. Future projects deemed critical will still be subject to regulatory, environmental and Indigenous consultation requirements.

Last week, TC Energy announced plans to expand its pipeline network with a 370-kilometre pipeline that stretches west to east called the Alberta Growth Connector, which would add a preliminary billion cubic feet per day of new capacity.

The Calgary-based company has invested more than $15 billion in its NGTL system.

Jean said he’s been in talks with TC over the last few weeks.

“They’re a great company and we’re looking forward to working with them to take advantage of what we have as a natural gas asset, which is an amazing opportunity for us if we move forward together,” said the minister. “We’re looking at the natural gas that goes outside of Alberta and the natural gas system that’s inside of Alberta, and we’re hoping to work with our partners to make it a better system.”

In a letter to the province obtained by CTV News Edmonton, TC Energy said its integrated NGTL-ATCO system provides the lowest cost for Albertans.

“We are concerned the government’s proposed policy direction could have significant, material and negative consequences for Albertans,” said the letter signed by François Poirier, TC Energy’s president and CEO.

“As the government’s own analysis acknowledged in the now-public cabinet brief, it could result, among other things, in increased costs for Alberta families and businesses and expose taxpayers to significant financial risk.”

TC Energy suggests that overriding integration would create significant market instability.

“We struggle to see how we can progress the new offering of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet per day announced on Nov. 16, if legislation overrides the integrated NGTL-ATCO system.”

In September, a report to the premier’s cabinet was leaked, recommending the province make headway on legislation to create two Crown corporations in an effort to meet the demand for oil production and AI data centres.

During her radio program “Your Province Your Premier,” Danielle Smith said it was “unlikely” the government would launch a Crown corporation to build out natural gas pipelines.

Alberta has an estimated 130 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves and produces about 60 per cent of Canada’s natural gas.

items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.3T in September as mortgage growth fell to a 25-year low, while consumer credit ran hot on rising distress borrowing.
items.body:
Canadian household debt is slowing in growth, but it doesn’t appear to be voluntary deleveraging. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit climbed in September, though mortgages are contributing less. The segment grew at one of the slowest paces in a quarter-century, even as consumer credit took off alongside rising distress borrowing.

Canadian Household Debt Hits $3.3 Trillion Even As Growth Slows

Annual growth of Canadian household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt climbed 0.3% (+$9.4 billion) to hit $3.3 trillion in September, 3.7% (+$119.3 billion) higher than last year. It’s a sharp deceleration from the 4.6% annual growth reported this time a year ago, suggesting household borrowing is slowing. Even at a slower pace, adding over $119 billion in a single year is hardly deleveraging. Households are just lightly tapping the brakes.

Canadian Mortgage Credit Growth Slows To Lowest Pace In 25 Years

Annual growth of Canadian mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage growth appears to be the big drag here. Outstanding mortgage credit rose 0.2% (+$4.9 billion) to $2.47 trillion in September, 3.5% (+$82.6 billion) from last year. This is the slowest annual growth for mortgage credit since mid-2001. In an economy as housing-dependent as Canada’s, a quarter-century low in mortgage expansion signals that buyers are either tapped out or stuck on the sidelines.

Distress Borrowing Keeps Consumer Credit Running Hot At $847 Billion

Annual growth of Canadian non-mortgage household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

One area of credit growth that continues to run hot is consumer credit. Households grew non-mortgage debt by 0.5% (+$4.5 billion) to $847.0 billion in September, up 4.5% (+$36.7 billion). While slower than August, the annual growth of this segment has been higher than usual over the past few years, sustaining levels the country hasn’t seen since mid-2010. Healthy credit growth can sometimes be a sign of strong consumers, but this isn’t one of those times.

Credit reporting bureaus are increasingly attributing growth to distress borrowing. Firms like TransUnion have noted that more borrowers are carrying higher balances as they use credit to make ends meet. Mortgage borrowers aren’t much better, with the bureau also explaining that a rising share of mortgage debt is due to accumulating balances, not originations.

Slowing headline growth may look like restraint on the surface, but it’s a more ominous sign. There are few signs of relief ahead, as the market expects higher borrowing costs.

items.title: M3’s Bernard talks CMAs, importance of recognizing top performers
items.description: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.content: <p>Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275163379725593.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) finally arrive this week – and as the event’s social media sponsor, M3 Financial Group is backing the brokers, lenders, and service providers shortlisted across multiple categories.

The event, set to take place at Rebel Toronto on November 25, will celebrate its 20th anniversary this year. Luc Bernard, chairman and chief executive officer of M3, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that paying tribute to the industry’s best performers was an essential part of ensuring the sector goes from strength to strength.

“We feel that it is of utmost importance to celebrate the mortgage broker industry and recognize the top performers,” he said. Being in a room with the sector’s highest achievers, he said, “obliges us to continue elevating our work year after year.”

The event draws nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and industry service providers across the country. Nominations closed in August, with the shortlisted Excellence Awardees published last month.

Brokers can be recognized regionally, with separate awards for Eastern Canada (Quebec and Ontario), the Maritimes and Atlantic Canada, and Western Canada, or by specialty – with awards for alternative, private lending, reverse mortgage and commercial brokers.

Brokerages and teams compete by size, alongside awards for national broker networks, national brokerages and new brokerages. On the lending side, BDMs and underwriters are recognized in both prime and specialist (alternative and private) categories. Industry service providers, innovators and employers of choice round out the field.

All you need to know about the award categories

Several awards put the spotlight on people. Twelve brokers are shortlisted for Young Achiever of the Year, 11 for The MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, and nine for The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year, (see CMP's full list of 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards excellence awardees here).

The fields vary in size. The regional broker awards each have 10 or 11 shortlisted brokers, while the private lending and commercial categories have seven each, the reverse mortgage category three, and the National Broker Network of the Year category four.

Sponsors have also put their names on individual awards, including The EQ Bank Award for Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages and The Grechi Carter Professional Corporation Award for Broker of the Year – Commercial. The Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, the programme's highest honour, has no shortlist and will be announced only on the night.

Brokers shine in challenging times

The industry’s top performers have shone in a challenging market this year, one that’s brought the importance of mortgage brokers into even sharper focus.

The ongoing trade war with the US, and price pressures caused by the US-Iran conflict, have weighed against the housing market outlook for 2026 as affordability challenges and rising interest rates also leave their mark.

But brokers are coming to the fore in turbulent times that have also seen a wave of mortgage renewals in 2025 and 2026 at much higher rates than the original contract.

Overall broker market share reached 38% last year, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s (MPC’s) most recent consumer survey – a jump of six percentage points from the year before.

Nearly two in five Canadians took out their most recent mortgage through a broker in 2025, a new high for the channel, with the share climbing to 48% among recent first-time buyers.

For M3, a key focus of the year has been broker education, with the aim of equipping brokers to be “the best that they can be for future Canadian homeowners.”

Bernard said the night is also a reminder of the bigger goal. “Let’s all work together to grow this industry, allowing more Canadians to trust brokers with the biggest purchase of their lives,” he said.

items.body:
For RFA Financial, returning as a sponsor of the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is not simply a matter of brand visibility — it is an expression of values the Toronto-based lender says are foundational to how it operates.

The awards, presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, return to Rebel Toronto on November 25 for their 20th anniversary, recognising outstanding work across 26 categories spanning broker, brokerage, lender, and industry segments.

The 2026 edition arrives at what CMP has described as one of the most structurally significant moments in the country's recent mortgage history, shaped by a record renewal wave and persistent affordability pressure from coast to coast.

Among the sponsors backing this year's programme is RFA Financial Inc., the parent company of RFA Mortgage Corporation and RFA Bank of Canada — the firm's prime and alternative lending subsidiaries, respectively.

RFA Mortgage Corporation is sponsoring the Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service award, a category that Cheryl Buhs, VP of National Sales (Prime) at RFA Financial, says carries particular meaning.

"Our sponsored award, the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy & Community Service, is especially meaningful to us," Buhs told Canadian Mortgage Professional. 

"Giving back to the communities we serve is an integral part of RFA's culture, and it's something we work to champion across the industry."

The recognition of community service within a business-focused awards programme reflects a broader shift visible at the CMAs in recent years.

Buhs said RFA sees its sponsorship as part of a continuing effort to hold up those contributions for wider visibility.

"Supporting this award is one small way we can shine a light on the people making a difference across our country and encourage others to do the same," she said.

Raising the bar across the industry

Frank Giacomini, VP of National Sales (Alternative) at RFA Financial, echoed the view that industry recognition has a practical effect on standards.

"Recognizing the hard work of our peers keeps our industry moving forward," said Giacomini.

"When we celebrate great work, we inspire everyone to raise the bar and find new ways to serve our communities and make homeownership more accessible for Canadians."

"It's been another great year of connecting with our industry partners, and we're grateful for the relationships and collaboration that make RFA what it is," she said.

"Thank you to everyone who continues to put their trust in us. We're excited for what 2027 holds and look forward to building on this year's momentum together."

Giacomini added that RFA's focus heading into the new year remains unchanged: deepening its value to the broker channel.

"RFA is always working to be the preferred lending partner for brokers, and this year has been no different," he said.

"As we close out 2026 and head into 2027, our focus remains the same — finding ways to better serve our broker partners and their clients."

items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank's SVP on sponsoring the CMAs, broker relationships, and a national expansion that crossed the Rockies
items.body:
When Tru Cooperative Bank agreed to sponsor this year's Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMA), the decision was grounded in something more straightforward than marketing arithmetic.

The federally regulated credit union, formerly known as First West Credit Union, has worked alongside mortgage brokers in British Columbia for more than 23 years — and sponsoring the industry's benchmark recognition event is, in the words of its senior vice-president of pricing and national expansion, Sundar Ramanathan, CFA, (pictured top) a chance to say thank you.

"We have worked with mortgage brokers in B.C. for more than 23 years, and mortgage brokers have played a huge role in our growth," he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Now, as we take our broker business across Canada as a federal credit union, sponsoring the Canadian Mortgage Awards is a chance to say thank you and celebrate the people who've helped us prove that there's an important place for cooperative banking in this industry."

The 2026 CMAs mark the programme's 20th anniversary, a milestone that coincides with one of the most structurally consequential periods in the Canadian mortgage market's recent history. 

The gala takes place November 25 at Rebel Toronto, spanning 23 competitive categories that recognise outstanding work from broker specialists in private lending and reverse mortgages to the teams and technology shaping the market's future.

Results are announced at the awards show and simultaneously published on the CMA website, with coverage in CMP magazine and across its digital channels. mpamag

Raising the bar

Ramanathan makes no distinction between celebrating excellence and improving the broader market.

As a lender that operates on cooperative principles — member-owned, profit-averse in the conventional sense — Tru Cooperative Bank regards recognition events as instruments of collective advancement.

"Mortgages are ultimately a people business," Ramanathan said.

"Great brokers bring advice, trust, and expertise to one of the biggest financial decisions Canadians make. As a cooperative, we believe we're stronger when we help each other succeed. Recognising excellence celebrates the people setting a high standard and raises the bar for the whole industry."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Tru Cooperative Bank in recognizing the Excellence Awardees of the Tru Cooperative Bank for National Brokerage of the Year. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/TCt6mK5FV9 https://t.co/M2N4rjG8LI — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

A landmark year for Tru

For Tru Cooperative Bank itself, 2026 has been a year of institutional transformation.

First West Credit Union announced on April 1 that it was officially a federally regulated credit union operating under the new legal name Tru Cooperative Bank, with regulatory oversight transferring from the BC Financial Services Authority to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), placing it under Canada's federal banking regulatory framework.

With this transition, Tru Cooperative Bank became the fourth federally regulated credit union in Canada since federal legislation introduced in 2012 enabled credit unions to operate nationally. 

The broker expansion followed quickly. In May, the organisation announced the expansion of its Mortgage Broker Centre into Ontario through a strategic partnership with MCAP, a Canadian mortgage lender and servicer.

Less than four months after becoming a federally regulated credit union and just 77 days after expanding into Ontario, Tru Cooperative Bank had already exceeded $100 million in approved mortgage volume. 

Provincial growth continued through the year. The move to extend the institution's broker reach deepened a national expansion that gained substantial momentum in Ontario, with Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba following, and Atlantic Canada identified as the next target market, according to Ramanathan. 

"Our message to brokers is simple: we're here for the long term," Ramanathan said.

"We have 80 years of history behind us, and while our national broker business is new, we aren't. We want to earn brokers' business for the long term by listening, staying competitive and consistent, and being a lender they genuinely like working with."

items.content: <p>EVP announces he'll end an illustrious career next month</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639310556202175047.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: EVP announces he'll end an illustrious career next month
items.body:
Scott McKenzie, executive vice president of residential mortgages at First National Financial LP in Toronto, Ontario, has announced he will retire at the end of December, drawing to a close one of the longest and most consequential careers in the history of Canada's non-bank lending sector.

McKenzie joined First National in 1989 as its fifth employee, months after co-founders Stephen Smith and Moray Tawse established the firm.

He went on to assume a mandate that cut across the full scope of residential mortgage operations — both origination and credit — an unusually broad combination in the industry that made him a defining figure in how the lender built and maintained its relationships with brokers nationwide.

First National distributes its residential mortgages exclusively through the broker channel.

Read more: Macklem to exit Bank of Canada as successor search begins

From the fifth employee to $100 billion in mortgages

Under his oversight, First National's residential portfolio grew to $100 billion in mortgages under administration (MUA), according to the company, while the team under his leadership expanded to more than 1,000 employees. That trajectory ran in close parallel with the broader rise of the broker channel in Canada.

According to Mortgage Professionals Canada, the share of Canadians obtaining their mortgage through a broker climbed to 38%, up six percentage points from the year prior, with first-time buyers driving the sharpest gains.

McKenzie captured his perspective on that relationship in a 2024 message to mark the company's 35th year in the broker channel: "We are grateful that mortgage brokers give First National the chance to compete, the opportunity to serve and the encouragement to grow and innovate. To all of our partners, thank you for your support."

Read more: Montreal fintech nesto names SVP to accelerate operational growth

A year of leadership transition

McKenzie's retirement is not the only succession underway at First National this year. In March, the company announced that president and chief executive Jason Ellis would also step down by year's end, following more than 22 years at the firm.

First National has not named a successor for McKenzie's role, nor provided a timeline for doing so.

items.title: Ontario regulator shuts Scarborough brokerage over $500K trust dispute
items.description: RECO takes action after complaints over frozen buyer deposits
items.content: <p>RECO takes action after complaints over frozen buyer deposits</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0319_637100048227359663.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RECO takes action after complaints over frozen buyer deposits
items.body:
The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) has revoked the registrations of a Scarborough real estate brokerage and its broker of record following multiple complaints that approximately $500,000 in buyer deposits was held against transactions that failed to close.

Luxury Homes World Inc., located at 700-305 Milner Avenue, Scarborough, Ontario, and its broker of record, Inthiran Swamy, had their registrations cancelled on November 17. Neither the brokerage nor Swamy may now trade in real estate in the province.

Accounts frozen and registrations revoked

RECO moved first with a freeze order on November 10, covering all accounts associated with Luxury Homes World, including its real estate trust account, under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002 (TRESA).

The step was taken to safeguard consumer funds and prevent further unauthorized movement of money.

The enforcement followed multiple complaints linked to approximately $500,000 in submitted deposits for transactions that did not complete.

RECO confirmed the investigation is continuing and that further regulatory action may follow. The regulator noted the freeze order was unrelated to its mandatory annual financial filings program, which all approximately 3,800 registered Ontario brokerages were required to complete as of October 1.

Buyers who paid deposits to the brokerage are urged to contact RECO directly; the regulator administers a consumer deposit insurance program that may provide recourse for lost funds.

The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has imposed conditions on the insurance agent licence of Victor Ferreira following a settlement over administrative penalties that went unpaid for more than six years. https://t.co/meZLsXW9k6 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 11, 2026

Part of a wider pattern of enforcement

The Luxury Homes World case extends a string of RECO enforcement actions that have unsettled Ontario's real estate sector over the past 12 months. \

In February, RECO took action against four Save Max brokerages in Mississauga after a forensic review found approximately $2.7 million had been improperly withdrawn from trust accounts.

Those actions followed RECO's December 2025 freeze of accounts at Scarborough-based HomeLife Today Realty Ltd., where a shortfall of approximately $580,000 was uncovered, and the August 2025 collapse of iPro Realty Ltd., which exposed a $10 million shortfall and triggered a government-ordered audit of RECO's regulatory approach.

As RECO pushes through its eight-point modernization plan in the wake of those failures, its administrator and acting chief executive, Jean Lépine, has framed the enforcement surge in unambiguous terms.

"It is about ensuring that a small number of bad actors do not undermine the integrity of the entire profession," Lépine said in March at the Ontario Real Estate Association's annual general meeting in Ontario.

The Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) has backed the tougher oversight. As RECO set an October deadline for mandatory annual brokerage financial filings, OREA president Kim Fairley welcomed the direction.

"OREA is thrilled to see RECO and the Government of Ontario heed our calls for increased financial oversight and trust account reforms for brokerages, which will go a long way towards building back trust in the regulator," Fairley previously said.
